page: Alibaba Cloud ecs.sn2ne.large is a general-purpose virtual machine deployed on the KVM hypervisor. It runs on the x86_64 architecture and is powered by an Intel Xeon E5-2682v4 processor clocked at 2.5 GHz. The server configuration provides 2 vCPUs across a single physical core using two hardware threads with dedicated CPU allocation. Memory is provisioned at 8.0 GB, establishing a standard 1:4 vCPU-to-memory ratio of 4.0 GB per vCPU. The instance does not include integrated local disk storage or hardware GPU accelerators, necessitating reliance on network-attached block volumes. Baseline network bandwidth is capped at 1 Gbps, and no complimentary public IPv4 addresses are assigned by default.

Benchmark results place the computational and memory throughput of this hardware generation in the lower percentiles compared to modern cloud standards. The instance recorded a Geekbench single-core score of 913.0 and a multi-core score of 1083.0, paired with a stress-ng single-core score of 1092.58 and multi-core score of 1442.69. Memory bandwidth tests yielded 10.65 GB/sec for uncached large-block reads and 9.53 GB/sec for writes. Application-level performance demonstrates adequate execution for modest scenarios, reaching 1.43 million Redis SET operations per second and 1.26 GB/sec in static web serving throughput.

From an infrastructure perspective, ecs.sn2ne.large represents an entry-level tier for dedicated execution where compute isolation is preferred over shared-core alternatives. However, the reliance on older Broadwell-era Intel architecture yields lower instructions per cycle and restricted memory bandwidth relative to newer instance families. The absence of included local storage also requires accounting for attached block storage performance and cost in overall architectural deployments.

This server type is suitable for non-intensive production and test workloads that fit within an 8 GB memory footprint. Representative deployment targets include low-traffic web servers, staging environments, basic Redis caching layers, microservices, and internal tooling tasks that do not demand high vector computing or intensive multi-threaded CPU throughput.
